lessons.title: Divide whole numbers and keep the remainder
lessons.summary: Divide whole numbers and keep the remainder
explanation: An expression combines values to produce another value. An operand is a value an operator works on. With integers, + adds, - subtracts, and * multiplies. Quoted text is not an integer expression.
Parentheses can group arithmetic: (2 + 3) * 4 adds first, then multiplies. Without those parentheses, multiplication happens before addition.
Integer division with / discards the fractional part toward zero. For positive values, 7 / 2 produces 3, not 3.5. Do not divide by zero.
The remainder operator % gives what is left after integer division: 7 % 2 is 1. A calculation does not change a variable unless its result is assigned.

lessons.title: Choose numeric types

lessons.title: Convert numbers deliberately
lessons.summary: Change measurement to 4.8. What does this conversion produce?
explanation: A cast explicitly requests a conversion, written with a type in parentheses: (int)value. Converting a fractional number to int truncates toward zero: 3.9 becomes 3 and -3.9 becomes -3.

checked asks integral arithmetic and supported conversions to report overflow instead of silently wrapping. Overflow means a result is outside the destination type’s representable range.

A directly overflowing constant conversion instead causes a compile-time error. Exception handling is taught later; for now, understand that this conversion fails.

lessons.title: Build and inspect strings
lessons.summary: Replace topic with "moon" before these two operations. What prints?
explanation: An interpolated string begins with $. Expressions inside braces are evaluated and inserted into the text, as in $"Score: {score}".

A string value is immutable. Methods such as ToUpperInvariant return another string; they do not rewrite the original variable’s value unless you assign that result.

ToUpperInvariant() takes no arguments and returns an uppercased string using invariant culture: fixed casing rules rather than the user’s current language settings. The receiver remains unchanged; a distinct new string object is not promised.

Length counts UTF-16 code units. An index in brackets starts at zero; text[0] reads the first code unit as a char. Some displayed characters use more than one code unit, so Length is not always a count of human-visible symbols.
Calling a method and ignoring its result leaves the original text unchanged. Store the returned value if you need it later.
